list.listitem: Close monitoring of growth parameters is essential to diagnosing failure to thrive (FTT). Measure and plot height/length, weight, and head circumference at every well child visit. C

If no clear cause is found after a thorough history and physical examination, attempt dietary management first, including prospective food diaries and weekly follow-up visits to monitor weight and caloric intake. C
Undertake laboratory evaluation of FTT only if guided by history and physical findings. C
Admission to the hospital is only warranted in cases of severe malnutrition, failure of outpatient management, or concern for child safety. C

background.definition: Failure to thrive (FTT; also called failure to gain weight, undernutrition, or growth faltering) is defined by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, US Department of Health and Human Services, as a crossing of 2 or more standard percentile lines in a standard growth chart. Other commonly used definitions include children below 2.3 percentile or below 80% of ideal weight-for-age, 2 standard deviations below the mean weight-for-age, or less than the fifth percentile for expected weight gain. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have recently recommended using the World Health Organization international growth charts for children younger than 24 months of age—WHO growth charts are available at https://www.cdc.gov/growthcharts.

list.listitem: Prospective studies from England suggest that 4% to 10% of infants will have poor weight gain (<fifth percentile of expected weight gain) some time in the first year of life.

Although many retrospective studies have suggested an increased risk of FTT in infants of lower socioeconomic status, prospective population-based studies have failed to find significant independent associations with social class or parental education.

FTT is usually identified in the first 2 years of life. In the past, FTT was subclassified into organic and nonorganic categories. More recent literature avoids these terms, acknowledging that the etiology is often multifactorial.
Infant behaviors such as weak suck or food avoidance are important, as are caregiver characteristics such as anxiety, depression, or increased response to infant feeding behaviors.
The extremes of either parental neglect or hypervigilance can lead to FTT.

Following an episode of moderate to severe diarrhea in a child living in a low resource setting, 24% had severe linear growth faltering in the next 3 months. Risk factors included younger age, acute malnutrition, need for hospitalization, non-dysenteric diarrhea, lower family income, fever, and co-morbidities.
The underlying cause of FTT is insufficient usable nutrition.

This can be due to: (1) insufficient intake (psychosocial problems, mechanical feeding difficulties), (2) inability to use calories (malabsorption, metabolic errors), or (3) increased metabolic needs, as in chronic disease.
The vast majority of infants with FTT do not have underlying chronic disease.

Differential.Differential_Features: Murmur, clubbing, cyanosis, sweating with feeds

list.listitem: See Definition section.
When FTT is suspected, the first step is a complete history and physical examination to look for specific medical causes.
Take a history of feeding patterns, amounts, and behaviors, including 1- to 3-day food recall diary; a past medical history; and developmental history.
Assess any family history of poor growth or genetic or endocrine disorders.

Take a careful social history, with emphasis on who lives in the household, who cares for the patient, mental state of parents, family stressors, food insecurity and amount of social support available.

Begin the physical examination with measuring and plotting weight, height, and head circumference. Preservation of normal head circumference suggests inadequate intake, whereas proportionate reduction of head circumference suggests congenital defects or metabolic disorders.
Identification of FTT requires serial measurements of weight, height, and head circumference over time on an age appropriate growth chart.
Look for dysmorphic features. Perform a careful cardiac, pulmonary, and neurologic examination, including assessment of suck-swallow coordination.

Examine skin, hair, and nails for evidence of malnutrition or vitamin deficiency, as well as abuse. Perform a genital examination for signs of abuse or neglect and carefully observe the parent-child interaction.
Investigate for signs and symptoms of food allergies including Cow's Milk Allergy.
Observe a feeding and consider a home visit by an appropriate health professional (e.g., public health nurse).

Consider laboratory evaluation when dietary management fails, or when the history and physical suggest a specific disease. See algorithm in . Potentially useful tests, if clinically indicated, include metabolic profile, CBC, thyroid studies, coagulation studies, and serum albumin. Consider echocardiography if murmur or congenital heart disease are clinically suspected.
In a study of hospitalized infants with FTT, only 1.4% of laboratory tests (36 of 2607) were diagnostically helpful.
Consider a skeletal survey if abuse is suspected.
See algorithm in .
FTT interventions appear most effective during the first 2 years of life.

algorithm.title: Failure to Thrive (FTT): Diagnosis. (Ultimately, Consider All Potential Causes of FTT in Each Patient, as Etiology Is Often Multifactorial.)

cell.label: Measure and plot weight, length, and head circumference. Is poor growth symmetric, or is the head circumference spared (asymmetric)?
Suggests congenital or metabolic causes. Are GI symptoms present (diarrhea, steatorrhea, abdominal pain)?
Consider malabsorption: cow's milk protein allergy, cystic fibrosis, celiac disease, biliary atresia, inflammatory bowel disease, disaccharidase deficiency, or chronic diarrhea present?
Consider sweat test, tissue transglutaminase (TTG), gamma-glutaryl transferase (GGT), specialist referral.
Likely cause of FTT. Confirm diagnosis and treat as indicated.

Look for signs of chronic disease, which could be leading to increased metabolic needs: prematurity, recurrent infections, cardiac or pulmonary disorders, malignancy, renal or liver disease, or hyperthyroidism (including laboratory testing if indicated). Chronic disease present?
Consider improper utilization of calories: inborn errors of metabolism, storage disorders, or growth hormone deficiency. Consider specialist referral.
Suggests inadequate caloric intake. Observe feeding. Are there mechanical feeding difficulties?
Likely cause of FTT. Treat as indicated.

Investigate for psychosocial problems. Food diary to look for poor diet, inappropriate foods, unusual diets. Observed feedings to look for behavioral problems or oral aversion. In-depth interviews to look for parental mental health disorders, neglect, poverty, incorrect formula preparation.
